Fist
fīst
n. (the closed hand; a measure of assault, of false religion, and of God's grasp)
From Old English fyst, the clenched hand. Scripture uses it three ways — as the instrument of a blow the law must assess, as the emblem of a fast that quarrels, and, in Agur's question, as the figure for the hand that holds the wind.

Biblical Definition

The law takes the closed hand seriously enough to legislate for it: “And if men strive together, and one smite another with a stone, or with his fist, and he die not, but keepeth his bed” (Exodus 21:18). A stone and a fist are named in one breath, because the law is interested in the harm and not in whether a weapon was picked up. Isaiah then puts the fist inside a religious observance, which is where it does the most damage: “Behold, ye fast for strife and debate, and to smite with the fist of wickedness: ye shall not fast as ye do this day, to make your voice to be heard on high” (Isaiah 58:4). A man can keep a real fast, in the right month, and have his prayer refused because of what his hand is doing to his brother. And Agur takes the same word into an unanswerable question: “Who hath ascended up into heaven, or descended? who hath gathered the wind in his fists? who hath bound the waters in a garment? who hath established all the ends of the earth? what is his name, and what is his son's name, if thou canst tell?” (Proverbs 30:4). The fist that holds the wind is the only fist worth fearing, and the question about His Son's name is answered in the Gospels.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) defines the fist as the hand clenched; the hand with the fingers doubled into the palm.

expand to see more

FIST, n. [Sax. fyst.] The hand clenched; the hand with the fingers doubled into the palm.

FIST, v.t. To strike with the fist. To gripe with the fist.

SMITE, v.t. [Sax. smitan.] To strike; to throw, drive or force against, as the fist or hand, a stone or a weapon.

FAST, v.i. To abstain from food, beyond the usual time; to omit to take the usual meals, for a time.

STRIFE, n. Exertion or contention for superiority; contest of emulation, either by intellectual or physical efforts; discord; contention.

Key Scripture

Exodus 21:18 — "And if men strive together, and one smite another with a stone, or with his fist, and he die not, but keepeth his bed:"

Isaiah 58:4 — "Behold, ye fast for strife and debate, and to smite with the fist of wickedness: ye shall not fast as ye do this day, to make your voice to be heard on high."

Proverbs 30:4 — "Who hath ascended up into heaven, or descended? who hath gathered the wind in his fists? who hath bound the waters in a garment? who hath established all the ends of the earth? what is his name, and what is his son's name, if thou canst tell?"

Job 16:12 — "I was at ease, but he hath broken me asunder: he hath also taken me by my neck, and shaken me to pieces, and set me up for his mark."

Modern Corruption

Fasting and other disciplines are treated as devices that oblige God, so that a man may keep the observance and never examine the hand.

expand to see more

Isaiah 58 is the standing rebuke to every transactional piety. The people are fasting correctly — the chapter grants that they seek God daily and delight to know His ways — and God refuses the fast because of the fist. The mechanism they trusted was: perform the discipline, obtain the hearing. Verse 4 breaks the circuit. Ye shall not fast as ye do this day, to make your voice to be heard on high. The rest of the chapter names the fast God chose: loose the bands of wickedness, deal thy bread to the hungry, bring the poor that are cast out to thy house.

The Roman system of merit is the historic large-scale case, and the Reformation named it. But the mechanism is native to the human heart and survives in any congregation. A man in a quarrel with his brother goes on a fast and expects the fast to count; a church raises its intensity in worship while a member's grievance is left unaddressed. Christ made the same point plainer still: leave thy gift before the altar, go thy way, first be reconciled to thy brother, and then come and offer. The fist has to open before the hands are lifted.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew egroph (H106), a fist; chophen (H2651), the hollow of the hand, a fist; tsum (H6685), a fast; matstsah (H4683), strife.

expand to see more

Hebrew egroph (H106) — a fist; only Exodus 21:18 and Isaiah 58:4, the blow and the fast.

Hebrew chophen (H2651) — the closed hand, a handful; Proverbs 30:4, the wind gathered in his fists.

Hebrew tsom (H6685) — a fast; the observance Isaiah's hearers kept correctly.

Hebrew rib (H7379) — a quarrel, contention; the strife and debate of Isaiah 58:4.

Greek kolaphizo (G2852) — to strike with the fist; Matthew 26:67, what they did to Christ.

Usage

"“With a stone, or with his fist” — the law weighs the harm, not the weapon."

"“The fist of wickedness” — a correct fast with a closed hand."

"“Gathered the wind in his fists” — the only fist worth fearing."
